## Answer: 13 (low confidence)

I could not derive or verify this from first principles, so the answer rests on a partial argument plus a recalled classification that I have not checked.

**Constraints I could verify:**
- **Chordal:** If H is not chordal, then every H-subdivision contains an induced cycle of length at least 4. Chordal graphs have unbounded clique-width and contain no such cycle, so they lie in the class and H fails P.
- **Claw-free:** Any subdivision of a graph containing an induced claw has a vertex with three pairwise nonadjacent neighbours, so claw-free graphs (unbounded clique-width, e.g. some line graphs) exclude all such subdivisions. So H cannot contain an induced claw.
- **2K₂-free and P₅-free:** Split graphs are (2K₂, C₄, C₅, P₅)-free and have unbounded clique-width, which rules out H containing induced 2K₂ or P₅.

**Recalled (unverified) classification:** I believe the known result is that the class has bounded clique-width exactly when H is an induced subgraph of the gem or of K₄. I could not confirm this from memory.

**Maximal graphs:** Under that classification:
- The gem (K₁ joined to P₄) has 7 edges. It contains P₄, paw, diamond and K₃ as induced subgraphs.
- K₄ has 6 edges and is not an induced subgraph of the gem.

So M = {gem, K₄} and the sum is 7 + 6 = 13.

ANSWER: 13
